intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: Livestock · Forest · Soil water · Farm management
Four units. After each unit there is a **5-question tap quiz** (20 items total). Score updates as you go.

units.title: Farm Management
units.intro: Farming is a business that uses scarce land, labour, capital and management. Goal: best possible output from what you have — not maximum output at any cost.

cards.title: 4.1.1 Agriculture and the farm
body: **Agriculture** = an industry that organises **land, capital, labour and management** to produce food and non-food products (fibre, hides, wool, flowers).

A **farm** = an economic unit (a business firm) that grows crops or raises livestock using land, capital, labour and management, aiming at **profit**, or, on a subsistence farm, at feeding the family.
**Eritrean examples:** a 1 ha family farm near Adi Keyh growing barley and taff with two oxen; a commercial dairy near Asmara; a banana farm near Tesseney; a layer farm near Keren.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Farm management
body: **Farm management** = the process by which a farmer **plans, organises, co-ordinates and controls** the farm's land, labour and capital to reach goals such as higher output or profit. In short: using **scarce resources with alternative uses** to get the best result year after year.
**Functions of a farm manager:**
- buy inputs and combine them; decide **what** crops and livestock to produce and **how**;
- raise money (saving, borrowing); plan and co-ordinate work;
- pay **wages, interest and rent**;
- **keep records** and use them;
- **innovate** (new varieties, methods);
- **bear the risk** and uncertainty of success or failure.
**Objectives:** a **commercial** farm maximises profit (or minimises cost per unit); a **subsistence** farm aims at **self-sufficiency** with few inputs.
**Problems in Eritrea:** small farms, traditional methods, little capital, slow adoption of innovations, poor input supply, low managerial skills, weak communication and markets.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Agriculture as an industry
body: Modern agriculture is more than farming: it includes the firms that **make and sell inputs** (seed, fertiliser, machinery), **process and market** products (dairies, mills, tanneries), and the services of **education, research, extension and market information**. In developing countries it is the **largest employer** and the main livelihood. It must also be **sustainable**: good for the environment as well as for income.

cards.title: 4.1.4 Resources and factors of production
body: **Economics** = the study of how people use **limited resources** to satisfy **unlimited wants**. Every farmer must decide: **what** to produce, **how** to produce it, and **how much**.

**Resources have three features:** they have **economic value** (you pay for them), they are **limited**, and they have **alternative uses** (so choosing one use means giving up another: the **opportunity cost**).
**Factors of production:**
- **Land**: the most important factor for a farmer.

- **Labour**: physical and mental work; skilled labour is **human capital**. Its productivity depends on hours, climate, skill, organisation, equipment and pay. Forms: hired (wage), contract (per task), **family**, **collective** (neighbours working together in turn, as at harvest).

- **Capital**: anything made by people and used in production: **fixed capital** lasts many years (tractor, store, milking machine); **working capital** is used up in one season (seed, fertiliser, cash for wages).
- **Management / entrepreneurship**: organising the other factors, making decisions, trying new ideas, carrying the risk.

**Resources vs resource services:** fertiliser, seed and water are **used up**; labour, implements and buildings give **services**. **Fixed resources** (buildings, machinery) do not change with output in the planning period; **variable resources** (seed, fertiliser) do.

cards.title: Four factors and their rewards
body: Land earns rent, labour wages, capital interest, management profit.

cards.title: Opportunity cost
body: The value of the next-best use you gave up. Land under taff cannot also be under vegetables this season. Always ask “instead of what?”

cards.title: Worked example
cards.problem: A plot can earn 8,000 Nfa under sorghum or 11,000 Nfa under irrigated tomatoes, but tomatoes need 2,000 Nfa extra water fees. Which wins on simple profit?

steps.text: Tomatoes win by 1,000 Nfa — if water is actually available and risk is acceptable.
Opportunity cost of choosing sorghum would be that 1,000 Nfa.

cards.answer: Opportunity cost of choosing sorghum would be that 1,000 Nfa.

cards.title: 4.1.5 The production function
body: A **production function** shows how output (**y**) depends on inputs (**x**) with a given technology. It can be shown as a **table**, a **graph** or an **equation**: y = f(x), or with many inputs y = f(x₁, x₂, …, xₙ). With **one variable input** the others are held fixed: y = f(x₁ | x₂, …, xₙ).
Farming is a **biological** process: the farmer controls fertiliser, seed and land, but **not** rainfall or sunshine.
**Key measures:**
- **Total product (TP)**: total output.
- **Average product (AP)** = TP ÷ x (output per unit of input).
- **Marginal product (MP)** = ΔTP ÷ Δx (extra output from one more unit of input). MP decides the best input level.
**Law of diminishing returns:** when more and more of one input is added to fixed amounts of others, the **extra output from each added unit eventually falls**.

cards.title: Calculating AP and MP
cards.problem: From Table 4.1 (wheat), N = 40 kg gives 11 quintals and N = 60 kg gives 18 quintals. Find the AP at 60 kg and the MP between 40 and 60 kg.

steps.text: AP = TP ÷ x = 18 ÷ 60 = 0.30 quintal per kg of N.

cards.answer: AP = 0.30 q/kg; MP = 0.35 q/kg (each extra kg of N in that range adds 35 kg of grain).

cards.title: The three stages of production
body: - **Stage I** (from zero until **MP = AP**, where AP is highest): TP and AP rise; the input is **under-used**, so use more. Not rational to stop here.
- **Stage II** (from MP = AP until **MP = 0**, where TP is highest): the **rational** stage; the best level lies here.
- **Stage III** (**MP negative**): adding input **reduces** TP. Irrational even if the input were free: you lose output **and** pay for the input.
In Table 4.2 MP rises up to the 3rd kg, then falls (diminishing returns from the 4th kg); MP is 0 a little after 6 kg and negative at 7 kg.

cards.title: How much fertiliser pays best? MVP = price
body: The best point in Stage II depends on **prices**. **Marginal value product (MVP) = MP × price of output**: the extra money from one more unit of input.
- MVP > price of input → **use more** (it pays).
- MVP < price of input → **use less**.
- **Profit is greatest where MVP = price of input.**
With maize at 5 Nakfa/kg and fertiliser at 15 Nakfa/kg (Table 4.3), MVP = 15 at **5 kg/ha**, so apply 5 kg/ha.
The same idea in output terms: produce up to where **marginal revenue (MR) = marginal cost (MC)**. MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ; for a small farm selling at the market price, MR = price.

cards.title: Finding the optimum fertiliser rate
cards.problem: Maize sells at 4 Nakfa/kg and fertiliser costs 16 Nakfa/kg. Using the MP column of Table 4.2 (4, 6, 8, 4, 3, 1, −1 for the 1st to 7th kg), how many kg should be applied?

steps.text: Compare with 16 Nakfa: the 1st to 4th kg each earn at least 16; the 5th earns only 12.
So stop after the 4th kg (MVP = price at 4 kg).

cards.answer: 4 kg/ha. A cheaper input or a dearer crop would push the optimum higher.

cards.title: Costs and revenue
body: - **Fixed costs (FC)** do not change with output and are paid even if nothing is produced: machinery and buildings (depreciation, interest, insurance), land tax, rent.
- **Variable costs (VC)** change with output: seed, fertiliser, pesticide, fuel, hired labour.

- **Total cost (TC) = FC + VC**. Per unit: **AFC = FC ÷ Q** (always falls), **AVC = VC ÷ Q**, **TAC (ATC) = TC ÷ Q**, **MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ**. AVC, TAC and MC first fall, reach a minimum and then rise; MC cuts AVC and TAC at their lowest points.
- **Total revenue (TR) = quantity × price**: a straight line for a farm that sells at the market price.
- **Net revenue (profit) = TR − TC.** It is greatest where **MR = MC**: produce one more unit while MC < MR; stop when MC > MR.

cards.title: Fixed or variable? Profit or loss?
cards.problem: A poultry farmer has yearly costs: depreciation of the house 6 000, interest on the loan for it 2 000, feed 30 000, chicks 8 000, vaccines 1 000, hired labour 9 000 Nakfa. He sells 9 000 trays of eggs at 7 Nakfa. Find FC, VC, TC and profit.

cards.title: How to produce: combining two inputs
body: Many mixes of two inputs can give the same output. An **iso-quant** joins all the combinations (for example of labour and capital) that give **one fixed output**. The rate at which one input can replace another is the **marginal rate of substitution**.
**Least-cost (best) combination:** MP of input 1 ÷ its price = MP of input 2 ÷ its price, i.e. **MP₁/P₁ = MP₂/P₂**: the last Nakfa spent on each input brings the same extra output.
In Table 4.4 (wage 50 Nakfa a day, capital rent 200 Nakfa a day) this happens at combination 5: MP of labour ÷ wage = 80 ÷ 50 = **1.6** = MP of capital ÷ rent = 320 ÷ 200.

cards.title: What to produce: two products
body: With fixed resources a farmer can shift land and labour between products. The **production possibility curve (PPC)** shows all combinations of two products that the resources can produce. Points **on** or **inside** it are possible; points **outside** are not.
**Marginal rate of product substitution (MRPS)** = how much of one product must be given up to get one more unit of the other.

**Best combination:** where the PPC just touches the highest **iso-revenue line** (all combinations giving the same TR = Qₘ × Pₘ + Q_w × P_w); algebraically, where the amount of maize given up per kg of extra wheat equals the price ratio P_wheat ÷ P_maize.

cards.title: Checking Table 4.5 with revenue
cards.problem: Wheat sells at 42 and maize at 24 Nakfa/kg. Compare the total revenue of plans D (600 wheat, 1 060 maize), E (800, 790), F (1 000, 440) and G (1 200, 0).
cards.answer: E and F tie at 52 560 Nakfa, the highest. The textbook picks F because there the substitution rate (1.75) equals the price ratio 42 ÷ 24 = 1.75; moving from E to F leaves revenue unchanged.

cards.title: Textbook checks in 4.1
body: - Equation 4.3 is printed the same as 4.2. With one variable input it should read **y = f(x₁ | x₂, …, xₙ)** (x₂ … xₙ held fixed).
- MRPS is defined once as ΔM/ΔW and once as ΔW/ΔM; Table 4.5 uses **Δmaize ÷ Δwheat**, compared with **P_wheat ÷ P_maize**.
- In Table 4.2 maize yields 10 kg with no fertiliser, so AP at 1 kg (14) is higher than later; this is why AP falls from the start in that table.

cards.title: Exam favourites from 4.1
body: - **Diminishing returns**: each extra bag of fertiliser adds less than the last.
- **Opportunity cost**: the value of the best alternative given up.
- **Stage II** is the rational stage; **MVP = price of input**; **MR = MC**.
- **Fixed vs variable** costs: insurance, depreciation, rent are fixed; fuel, seed, fertiliser, casual labour are variable.
- Production function → **how much**; iso-quant → **how** to produce; PPC → **what** to produce.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are correct about input-product relationship in stage three (III) **except**;

options.C: Average product and total product declines.
options.D: It is zone of rational production.

cards.why: Stage III of production is the 'Irrational Zone'. In this stage, the Marginal Product (MP) becomes negative, and Total Product (TP) starts to decline. A rational producer would never operate in this stage because adding more input actually reduces output.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The law of diminishing returns states that, as more units of a variable input (e.g. fertilizer) are added to a fixed input (land):

options.C: each extra unit eventually adds less and less to total output
options.D: output always increases by the same amount

cards.why:
**Step 1:** At first extra fertilizer may raise yield strongly.

**Step 2:** After a point, each additional bag gives a smaller increase in yield (marginal product falls).

**Step 3:** Answer: each extra unit eventually adds less and less.

**Tip:** A farmer should stop adding input when the value of the extra output equals the cost of the extra input.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Farm records and accounts
body: **Why keep records?** To see the farm's **strong and weak points**, find problems and correct them, show a lender that a loan can be repaid, help the farmer think and decide systematically, and give government data for policy.
**Good records are** useful, correctly collected, designed for the user, and **simple**.
**A complete set:** physical inventory, depreciation, accounts receivable and payable, receipts, expenditure, labour, machinery and production records.

- **Inventory (asset register)**: a list, at least **once a year**, of everything the farm owns, with quantities and money values (land, buildings, machinery, livestock, stored grain, supplies), after depreciation.

- **Depreciation**: loss of value of machinery, vehicles, tools and buildings through **age, wear and tear, and obsolescence**. It is a **non-cash cost** written off each year: **annual depreciation = (cost price − salvage value) ÷ expected life**.

- **Income and expenditure**: keep farm and household money **separate**; record produce eaten at home or given as rations. Sources: bank statements, cash analysis book, petty cash book, wage book, cheque counterfoils, invoices and receipts.
- **Journal**: the book in which **all transactions** are recorded **in date order**.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Production, labour and machinery records
body: - **Crop records**: field number, area, soil test, variety, seed, fertiliser, weeding, pest control, yield.
- **Livestock records**: feed, medicine, dosing, marketing costs; for each animal milk yield, calving dates, weaning weight, weight gain, wool.
- **Labour records**: workers, contracts, wages, rations, medical costs, loans, leave.
- **Machinery records**: model, age, book value, repairs, services, hours worked, insurance.
They show where yields or costs go wrong, e.g. a cow whose milk falls after every calving, or a field that always yields less.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Financial statements
body: A full set = **balance sheet**, **income statement** and **cash-flow statement**.
**Balance sheet**: the financial position on **one date** (e.g. 31 December). **Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital (net worth).**

- **Assets** (what the farm owns), by **liquidity**: **current** (cash, bank, unsold produce, supplies, debtors; turned into cash within 12 months) and **fixed / non-current** (land, buildings, machinery, orchards, breeding stock; most are depreciated).
- **Liabilities** (what it owes): **current** (due within a year: accounts payable, interest, wages, tax) and **long-term** (loans for tractors, buildings).
- **Net worth = assets − liabilities**: what the owner would keep after selling everything and paying all debts. Negative net worth = **insolvent**.

**Income statement (profit and loss)**: revenue, expenses and **net income or loss** over a **period**. Only items that change capital count: a bank loan is **not** revenue; buying a tractor is **not** an expense (its depreciation is).

**Cash-flow statement**: only **actual cash** in and out, month by month, in the month paid or received: operating, capital and non-farm income; operating and capital spending, debt repayments, household spending. **Depreciation is not included** (no cash moves).

cards.title: An income statement
cards.problem: In January Alem Farm sold crops for 2 000 Nakfa and paid rent 500, salaries 200 and fertiliser 200. It also borrowed 1 000 from the bank and bought a 3 000 Nakfa pump (life 10 years, no salvage). Find the net income for January.

steps.text: Revenue = crop sales = 2 000 (the loan is not revenue).
Expenses = 500 + 200 + 200 = 900, plus one month of pump depreciation = 3 000 ÷ 10 ÷ 12 = 25.

cards.answer: 1 075 Nakfa (the textbook's 1 100 leaves out the pump). The 3 000 pump purchase appears in the cash flow, not as an expense.

cards.title: Textbook checks in 4.2
body: - Under "Expenses" the text says "the **revenue** is equal to the value of goods and services used up"; it means the **expense**.
- In cash flow, expenditure is recorded in the month of **payment** (the text says "receipt").
- Long-term liabilities are given as debts of "more than five years". Usually any debt due after **more than one year** is non-current (1–5 years is sometimes called intermediate).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a classical agricultural production function, which stage of production represents the 'rational zone' where the profit-maximizing input level is located?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Stage I is a zone of under-utilization where input efficiency is still rising. Stage III is a zone of waste where adding more inputs decreases total product (negative MP). Stage II is the only rational zone of production because the marginal product is positive but decreasing, and the optimal profit-maximizing point (where MVP = Px) lies within its boundaries.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the rational zone is **Stage II**.

cards.q: The main purpose of keeping farm records is to ____.

options.B: help the farmer plan, measure profit or loss and make better decisions

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Records show inputs, outputs, costs and income.

**Step 2:** From them the farmer can calculate profit or loss and compare enterprises.

**Step 3:** This supports planning, borrowing and decisions.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A complete inventory of physical assets and their monetary values should be prepared by a farm business at least:

options.E: Only when the farm is sold

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
a physical inventory is a detailed list of all physical assets and their monetary values. It is standard accounting practice that this inventory should be prepared at least once a year to assess the net worth and financial position of the farm.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the inventory must be prepared at least **Once a year**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Under what conditions is a farm said to be insolvent or bankrupt on its balance sheet?

options.A: When total revenues are lower than variable costs.
options.B: When net worth or owner's equity is negative.
options.C: When current assets exceed long-term liabilities.
options.D: When there is a net loss on the income statement.
options.E: When no physical inventory is kept.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
A balance sheet reflects the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Net worth (owner's equity) is calculated as Assets minus Liabilities. If a farm's total liabilities (debts) exceed its total assets, the net worth becomes negative, which means the farm is insolvent or bankrupt.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, insolvency occurs **When net worth or owner's equity is negative**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following are considered non-cash costs and are therefore excluded from a cash-flow statement?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
A cash-flow statement records only actual cash inflows and cash outflows at the time they occur. Depreciation is an accounting entry representing the loss of value of an asset over time and does not involve any actual cash transaction. Therefore, it is excluded from cash-flow statements.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the excluded non-cash cost is **Machinery depreciation**.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Planning and budgeting
body: Farming is complex, so it must be **planned**. Three parts:

- **List resources and needs**: **land** (ownership: village, government or private; fertility; cultivable area; distance to market), **labour** in **person-days** (1 person-day = an average person working **8 hours**), **capital** (available vs required; the gap may be borrowed), **management** (experience, training, interest).
- **Land-use plan**: which land is for crops, vegetables, livestock, woodlot.
- **Budget**: a written plan in **physical and money terms**, based on forecasts, past records and experience. It is a **management aid**, not a rigid rule; update it when prices or rain change.
**Partial budget**: for a **small change** (a new variety on 1 ha); includes **only the costs and returns that change**. Adopt the change if the extra income is greater than the extra cost.
**Complete budget**: for the **whole farm** or a whole enterprise; useful when starting a farm or comparing enterprises.

cards.title: A full partial budget
cards.problem: A farmer puts 1 ha of his barley land under a new wheat variety: extra costs 2 400, wheat revenue 6 000 Nakfa (Table 4.9). The hectare used to give barley worth 2 500 Nakfa with costs of 900 Nakfa. Is the change worthwhile?

steps.text: Gains: new revenue 6 000 + barley costs saved 900 = 6 900.
Losses: new costs 2 400 + barley revenue given up 2 500 = 4 900.

cards.answer: Yes: profit rises by 2 000 Nakfa. Table 4.9 shows +3 600 because it leaves out the barley given up; a real partial budget counts both what is gained and what is lost.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Decision-making
body: The purpose of planning and budgeting is **better decisions**. A decision based on a written plan beats a guess. In Table 4.9 the extra revenue (6 000) exceeds the extra cost (2 400) by **3 600 Nakfa**, so the change is accepted.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Implementation
body: Carry out the plan: get the seed and fertiliser in time, organise labour (family, hired, wenfera), follow the calendar of operations.

cards.title: 4.3.4 Monitoring
body: Watch the work as it happens and **keep records** (dates, inputs, costs, yields) so the results can be compared with the plan.

cards.title: 4.3.5 Evaluation and appraisal
body: At the end of the season **compare planned and actual profit**, find the reasons for any gap (rain, prices, pests, management) and use the lessons in next year's plan.

cards.answer: No: the family can just manage (4 person-days to spare), but a sick day would make it tight.

cards.title: 4.4.1 Community-based organisations
body: Farmers have always pooled work at **sowing, weeding, harvest and threshing**: in Eritrea neighbours help each other in turn (**wenfera**). **Community-based organisations (CBOs)** are membership groups of people, usually living near each other, who join for **common interests**: women's groups, savings and credit groups, youth clubs, farmer co-operatives.

**At village level** CBOs pool resources for shared goals: building **roads, schools, clinics and dams**, **soil and water conservation** (terraces, enclosures), clean water projects. They make development **owned, open and accountable** to the community.

cards.title: 4.4.2 Co-operatives
body: A **co-operative** = an **autonomous association** of people who unite **voluntarily** to meet common economic, social and cultural needs through a **jointly owned, democratically controlled** enterprise. It is owned and run by and for its members; it is **not a charity** and **not state-directed**.
**Values:** self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, solidarity; members value honesty, openness, social responsibility and caring for others.
**Benefits:** jobs and steady income, local investment, informed local leaders, less migration, bargaining power, cheaper inputs.
**Types:**
- **Producer**: owned by producers (vegetable growers).
- **Consumer**: shops selling to members at fair prices.
- **Marketing**: members sell together for better prices (onion or banana producers' associations).
- **Credit unions (savings and credit)**: members save monthly and borrow at low interest in proportion to their savings.
- **Service**: bulk purchase of feed, fertiliser, seed and chemicals, sold to members at fair prices.

cards.title: Note on surplus sharing
body: The textbook says members share the surplus "based on the size of the investment". In the international co-operative principles, capital gets only **limited** interest; the surplus is shared mainly **in proportion to each member's business with the co-operative** (how much milk or produce they sold through it, or bought from it). That is what makes a co-operative different from a company.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Unlike private corporations where voting power is proportional to the number of financial shares owned, cooperatives follow the democratic principle of equality: "one member, one vote," regardless of how much capital a member has contributed.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the core democratic principle is **One member, one vote**.

tips.text: Agriculture can be defined as an industry involving the organization of resources such as land, capital, labour and management for the production of food and raw materials.

questions.q: A vegetable farm near Asmara owns a tractor, an irrigation system and a farm store building. Which one of the following items would be classified as working capital and NOT as fixed capital on this farm?

options.A: Fertilizer purchased for the coming tomato season
options.C: Irrigation system fitted with a diesel pump
options.D: Farm store building for harvested vegetables

why: **Recall the definition of capital.** Capital is the human-made factor of production. The unit divides it into fixed capital (assets used over many years) and working capital (cash or inputs used up in a single production cycle).

**Apply the test of a single production cycle.** Fixed capital such as tractors, buildings and irrigation systems gives service over many years and depreciates over time. Working capital such as seeds, fertilizers and pesticides is consumed within one season.

**Screen each option.** B (tractor) and C (irrigation system) are listed in the unit as fixed capital, and D (farm store building) is also a building used over many years. None of them is used up in one season.
**Select and conclude.** Only A, fertilizer for the coming tomato season, is an input used up inside a single production cycle, so it is working capital and not fixed capital.

questions.q: On a dairy farm in the Eritrean highlands, which one of the following is working capital rather than fixed capital?

why: **State the classification rule.** Working capital is cash or inputs that are used up in a single production cycle; fixed capital is used over many years.
**Check each item.** The milking shed and the milking machine are used over many years, so both are fixed capital.
**Test the remaining option.** Animal feed is consumed by the cows within the current cycle and must be replaced continuously, so it is used up in one cycle.
**Conclude.** Animal feed for the current cycle is working capital, therefore the answer is A.

**Identify the single-cycle input.** Maize seed is planted and used up within one production cycle, exactly like the seeds and fertilizers named in the unit.
**Conclude.** Maize seed is working capital, so the answer is C.

questions.q: A farmer at Keren is considering replacing the local wheat variety on one hectare with a new high-yielding variety. The change would raise seed cost by $$30\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and fertilizer cost by $$9\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, and it would reduce the cost of hired labour for weeding by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. Yield would rise by $$12\text{ quintals}$$, each selling at $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$, but the crop would no longer be sold as local seed, which used to bring an extra $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Using a partial budget, decide whether the farmer should adopt the new variety, and state the net change in returns.
questions.answer: The farmer should NOT adopt the new variety, because Added Returns + Reduced Costs ($$16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$) are less than Added Costs + Reduced Returns ($$42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$); the change would make returns worse by $$25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.
why: **Name the tool and its decision rule.** This is a minor single-enterprise change on one hectare, so a partial budget is the correct tool. The rule from the unit is: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.
**Compute total added returns.** The extra yield is $$12\text{ quintals} \times 1\,200\text{ Nakfa} = 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Added Returns $$= 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compute total reduced costs.** Hired weeding labour falls by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Reduced Costs $$= 2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. The left-hand side is $$14\,400 + 2\,500 = 16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Compute the added costs and reduced returns.** Added Costs are extra seed plus extra fertilizer: $$30\,000 + 9\,800 = 39\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$. Reduced Returns are the lost local-seed premium of $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. The right-hand side is $$39\,800 + 3\,000 = 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Compare and conclude.** $$16\,900\text{ Nakfa} < 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, so the right-hand side is larger. The change fails the partial-budget test by $$42\,800 - 16\,900 = 25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, and the farmer should not adopt the new variety.

questions.q: A farmer at Massawa plans to buy a small diesel pump to irrigate one hectare of vegetables. The pump costs $$18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and annual fuel and maintenance add $$4\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, while it would save $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year in hired watering labour. Extra vegetables worth $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year would be produced. Use a partial budget to decide whether the pump should be bought, and give the net change per year.
questions.answer: Buy the pump: Added Returns + Reduced Costs = $$21\,000 + 7\,000 = 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ exceeds Added Costs = $$22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, giving a net gain of $$5\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year.
why: **Identify the tool and rule.** Buying one new tool for one hectare is a minor change, so use a partial budget: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.
**Add up the benefit side.** Added Returns are the extra vegetables, $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; Reduced Costs are the saved watering labour, $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Total $$= 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Add up the cost side.** Added Costs are the pump price plus fuel and maintenance: $$18\,000 + 4\,500 = 22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. There are no reduced returns in this case.
**Compare and conclude.** $$28\,000 > 22\,500$$, so the pump passes the test by $$28\,000 - 22\,500 = 5\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year and should be bought.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands is considering joining a service cooperative instead of buying inputs alone. Membership costs $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year, and fertilizer bought through the cooperative is $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$ cheaper per year for the farm. However, seed must now be bought only from the cooperative, which is $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year more expensive, and cooperative members may not receive a $$500\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year input subsidy from a local buyer. Use a partial budget to decide whether to join.
questions.answer: Join the cooperative: Added Returns + Reduced Costs = $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$ exceeds Added Costs + Reduced Returns = $$2\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, giving a net gain of $$1\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year.
why: **Set up the partial budget.** Joining a cooperative changes only input purchase, a minor change, so apply: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.
**List the benefit side.** There is no extra output, so Added Returns $$= 0$$. Reduced Costs are the cheaper bulk fertilizer, $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$. Total benefit $$= 4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**List the cost side.** Added Costs are the membership fee of $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ plus the dearer seed of $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$. Reduced Returns are the lost $$500\text{ Nakfa}$$ subsidy. Total $$= 700 + 1\,200 + 500 = 2\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compare and conclude.** $$4\,300 > 2\,400$$, a net gain of $$1\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year, so the farmer should join the cooperative.

questions.q: On 31 December a farm business near Asmara reports current assets of $$25\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and long-term assets of $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Its current liabilities are $$8\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and its long-term bank loan is $$12\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Calculate the farm's net worth (capital). (b) State whether the farm is solvent, and explain what the balance sheet would have to show for the farm to be insolvent.
questions.answer: (a) Net worth = $$100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (b) The farm is solvent because net worth is positive; it would be insolvent only if total liabilities exceeded total assets, giving a negative net worth.
why: **State the balance-sheet equation.** A balance sheet reflects the financial position on a specific date and follows the accounting equation $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital (Net Worth)}$$.
**Total the assets.** Current assets plus long-term assets: $$25\,000 + 75\,000 = 100\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Total the liabilities.** Current liabilities plus long-term liabilities: $$8\,000 + 12\,000 = 20\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Solve for net worth.** Rearranging the equation gives Net Worth $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities} = 100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Interpret solvency.** Net worth is positive ($$80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$), so assets exceed liabilities and the farm is solvent. It would be insolvent (bankrupt) only if liabilities exceeded assets, that is, if net worth were negative.

questions.q: A farm business in Keren has cash of $$6\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, unsold crops valued at $$19\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, land and buildings valued at $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, a current debt of $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and a long-term loan of $$13\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Use the accounting equation to find the net worth, and identify which items are current assets.
questions.answer: Net worth = $$100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; the current assets are the cash ($$6\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$) and the unsold crops ($$19\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$).
why: **Write the accounting equation.** $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital (Net Worth)}$$, so Net Worth $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities}$$.

**Separate current and long-term assets.** Cash and unsold crops are convertible to cash within $$12\text{ months}$$, so they are current assets: $$6\,000 + 19\,000 = 25\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Land and buildings are long-term assets of $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Total assets and liabilities.** Assets $$= 25\,000 + 75\,000 = 100\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; liabilities $$= 7\,000 + 13\,000 = 20\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compute net worth.** Net Worth $$= 100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

questions.q: A farm business at Massawa lists total assets of $$65\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and a net worth of $$47\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Find its total liabilities. (b) If the long-term bank loan is $$11\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, what is the value of the current liabilities?
questions.answer: (a) Total liabilities = $$18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (b) Current liabilities = $$18\,000 - 11\,000 = 7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
why: **Start from the accounting equation.** $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Net Worth}$$, therefore Liabilities $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Net Worth}$$.
**Substitute the given values.** Liabilities $$= 65\,000 - 47\,000 = 18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Split liabilities by maturity.** Long-term liabilities are debts such as long-term bank loans, and current liabilities are debts due within one year; together they make up total liabilities.
**Find current liabilities.** Current liabilities $$= 18\,000 - 11\,000 = 7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

questions.q: A maize farmer near Barentu applies bags of nitrogen fertilizer to a fixed plot of land. The response of the crop is: with $$3$$ bags the total product is $$22\text{ quintals}$$, with $$4$$ bags it is $$28\text{ quintals}$$, with $$5$$ bags it is $$32\text{ quintals}$$ and with $$6$$ bags it is $$34\text{ quintals}$$. Maize sells at $$900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal and each bag of fertilizer costs $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Compute the marginal product of the fourth, fifth and sixth bags. (b) Compute the Marginal Value Product for each of those bags. (c) State the profit-maximizing number of bags and explain why applying one more bag would reduce profit.
questions.answer: (a) MP: 4th bag $$= 6$$, 5th bag $$= 4$$, 6th bag $$= 2\text{ quintals}$$. (b) MVP: 4th $$= 5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$. (c) The profit-maximizing level is $$5$$ bags, because the 5th bag's MVP ($$3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$) still exceeds the input price ($$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$) while the 6th bag's MVP ($$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$) is below it, so the 6th bag would cost more than it returns.
why: **State the two formulas needed.** Marginal Product is $$\text{MP} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$ and Marginal Value Product is $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$, where $$P_y$$ is the unit price of the output. Profit is maximized where $$\text{MVP} = P_x$$.

**Compute the marginal products.** Fourth bag: $$28 - 22 = 6\text{ quintals}$$. Fifth bag: $$32 - 28 = 4\text{ quintals}$$. Sixth bag: $$34 - 32 = 2\text{ quintals}$$. MP is falling, which is the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns in action.

**Compute the marginal value products.** $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times 900\text{ Nakfa}$$. Fourth bag: $$6 \times 900 = 5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$. Fifth bag: $$4 \times 900 = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$. Sixth bag: $$2 \times 900 = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Compare each MVP with the input price.** The price of the input is $$P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ per bag. The fourth bag adds $$5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$ of value for $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, the fifth adds $$3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, and the sixth adds only $$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Identify the profit-maximizing level.** The fifth bag still gives $$\text{MVP} = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa} > P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so it is worth applying. The sixth bag gives $$\text{MVP} = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa} < P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so it is not worth applying. The profit-maximizing level is therefore $$5$$ bags.

**Explain the loss from over-application.** At the sixth bag the farmer pays $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and receives output worth only $$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, a net loss of $$200\text{ Nakfa}$$. All the levels examined still lie in Stage II, where MP is positive but falling; pushing inputs until MP becomes negative would enter Stage III, the irrational zone of waste.

questions.q: A teff farmer in the Eritrean highlands applies units of fertilizer to a fixed plot. The total product is $$26\text{ quintals}$$ at $$2$$ units, $$30\text{ quintals}$$ at $$3$$ units, $$32\text{ quintals}$$ at $$4$$ units and $$33\text{ quintals}$$ at $$5$$ units. Teff sells at $$900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal and each unit of fertilizer costs $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Find the marginal product and the Marginal Value Product of each additional unit and state the profit-maximizing number of units.
questions.answer: MP: 3rd unit $$= 4$$, 4th $$= 2$$, 5th $$= 1\text{ quintal}$$. MVP: 3rd $$= 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 4th $$= 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 900\text{ Nakfa}$$. The profit-maximizing level is $$2$$ units, because the 3rd unit's MVP is already below the $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ input price.
why: **Recall the formulas.** $$\text{MP} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$, $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$, and profits are maximized where $$\text{MVP} = P_x$$.
**Compute the marginal products.** 3rd unit: $$30 - 26 = 4$$. 4th unit: $$32 - 30 = 2$$. 5th unit: $$33 - 32 = 1\text{ quintal}$$.

**Compute the marginal value products.** At $$P_y = 900\text{ Nakfa}$$: 3rd $$= 4 \times 900 = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 4th $$= 2 \times 900 = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 1 \times 900 = 900\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compare with the input price.** Every additional unit from the 3rd onward has $$\text{MVP} < P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so none of them pays for itself. The farmer should stop at $$2$$ units.
**Conclude.** The profit-maximizing quantity is $$2$$ units of fertilizer, and each unit beyond that would reduce total profit.

questions.q: A sorghum farmer at Keren is offered subsidized fertilizer at $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ per bag, while sorghum sells at $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal. Total product is $$18\text{ quintals}$$ with $$3$$ bags, $$25$$ with $$4$$ bags, $$30$$ with $$5$$ bags and $$33$$ with $$6$$ bags. Compute the marginal product and the Marginal Value Product of the fourth, fifth and sixth bags and recommend the profit-maximizing number of bags.
questions.answer: MP: 4th $$= 7$$, 5th $$= 5$$, 6th $$= 3\text{ quintals}$$. MVP: 4th $$= 4\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 3\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 2\,100\text{ Nakfa}$$. The profit-maximizing level is $$6$$ bags, since even the 6th bag's MVP exceeds the $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ price.
why: **State the decision rule.** Add input while $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$ exceeds the input price $$P_x$$, and stop at the level where the two are equal.
**Compute marginal products.** 4th bag: $$25 - 18 = 7$$. 5th bag: $$30 - 25 = 5$$. 6th bag: $$33 - 30 = 3\text{ quintals}$$.

**Compute marginal value products.** At $$P_y = 700\text{ Nakfa}$$: 4th $$= 7 \times 700 = 4\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 5 \times 700 = 3\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 3 \times 700 = 2\,100\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compare with the input price.** All three MVPs exceed $$P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so the 4th, 5th and 6th bags all add more value than they cost.
**Conclude.** Within the range given the farmer should apply all $$6$$ bags; the optimum would only be reached later, at the first bag whose MVP falls to $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

questions.q: Management (entrepreneurship) is described as the factor of production that combines land, labour and capital. Explain why management is regarded as the coordinating force among the other three factors of production, and contrast the main management objective of a commercial farm in Eritrea with that of a subsistence farm.
questions.answer: Management coordinates the other factors because it is the only human resource that combines land, labour and capital, makes the business decisions through planning, implementation and control, and bears all the risks of success or failure. A commercial farm aims at profit maximisation or cost minimisation, while a subsistence farm aims at household self-sufficiency rather than profit.
why: **Identify what each factor can and cannot do alone.** Land (soil, water and climate) has a fixed supply and is immobile; labour is the physical and mental contribution of humans; capital is the human-made asset set, either fixed or working. None of these three can decide by itself how much of the others to use.

**State the function of management.** Management is the human resource responsible for combining land, labour and capital, making the business decisions, and bearing all the risks of success or failure. It is therefore the decision-making and organisational factor.

**Explain the coordinating role.** The farm manager performs the functions of planning, implementation and control. Planning decides the enterprise and input levels, implementation organises land, labour and capital into actual production, and control compares results with the plan, so the three physical factors are only brought together and adjusted through management.

**State the commercial-farm objective.** On a commercial farm the main objective is the maximisation of profit or the minimisation of production costs, so decisions are driven by returns compared with costs.

**State the subsistence-farm objective and conclude.** On a subsistence farm the main objective is not profit but achieving household self-sufficiency, so the same resources are organised to feed the household first. In both cases, however, it is management that decides, bears the risk, and coordinates land, labour and capital.

questions.q: A farmer near Asmara has fertile land, six family workers and a tractor, yet the farm makes a loss. Using the factors of production, explain which factor is most likely to be the missing or weak element, and justify your answer with the functions of a farm manager.
questions.answer: The weak factor is management (entrepreneurship): land, labour and capital are all present, but without effective planning, implementation and control the resources are not combined into a profitable plan.
why: **List the four factors.** Production relies on land, labour, capital and management. The farm already has land (fertile soil), labour (six family workers) and capital (a tractor).
**Recall the functions of a farm manager.** The functions of a farm manager are divided into planning, implementation and control.

**Locate the gap.** Having resources is not the same as using them well: choosing what to produce, how much input to apply and how to check results are all planning, implementation and control decisions, which belong to management.
**Conclude.** The missing element is management, because it is the factor responsible for combining land, labour and capital and for bearing the risk of the outcome.

questions.q: Two farms near Keren each hold the same area of land and hire the same number of workers. Farm X sells its whole harvest on the market; Farm Y keeps most of its harvest for its own household and sells only a small surplus. Using the factors of production, explain how the two farms differ in their management objective and in the risk each manager bears.
questions.answer: Farm X is a commercial farm whose objective is maximisation of profit or minimisation of production costs, so its manager bears full market-price risk; Farm Y is a subsistence farm whose objective is household self-sufficiency, so its manager bears mainly production risk and takes little market risk.
why: **Recognise that the resource base is identical.** Both farms use the same land and the same quantity of labour, so the difference must lie in the management factor rather than in the physical factors.
**Classify Farm X.** Selling the whole harvest on the market is commercial farming, where the main objective is the maximisation of profit or the minimisation of production costs.
**Classify Farm Y.** Consuming most of the harvest at home means the main objective is not profit but achieving household self-sufficiency.

**Compare the risks borne.** Management is the factor that bears all risks of success or failure. Farm X's manager carries price and market risk on the whole output, whereas Farm Y's manager is largely shielded from price risk and mainly faces weather, pest and yield risk.
**Conclude.** Identical land and labour produce different decisions because the management objective differs: profit maximisation on Farm X and household self-sufficiency on Farm Y.
